_about: The one place for the core rules' version and change history. tools/build-website.py reads it for the core-rules page and the changelog. rulesVersion and rulesUpdated change only when the rules (mechanics) change; a website or wording update adds a 'site' entry and leaves them alone. rulesVersion is null until the author picks a numbering scheme.

changes.title: Dominion: send damaged ships for repairs
items: A fleet with damaged ships shows where best to mend them, counting the trip and the repair: a drydock fixes everything at once, a station 2 hull a turn, any other world of yours 1. It also shows how many turns that takes.

Send for repairs splits off the damaged ships (the sound ones and the admiral stay) and sends them there. In a battle, they withdraw first. Repair, then rejoin this fleet brings them back to the fleet once they're whole, following it if it has moved.

changes.title: Dominion: call a coalition against the Wardens
items: While the Wardens are awake, the Wardens card on the Objectives tab can call a coalition. Pick the Heart or one of its Nodes, and see which powers will come: free if they like you, for credits if they're lukewarm, or not at all, with the reason.

Members send their strongest war fleets, up to 60% of their warships, and hold the target with you for 20 turns or until it falls, without withdrawing. When it falls, everyone who fought it thinks better of each other. One call every 10 turns.
How to play and the strategy guide mention it.

changes.title: Dominion: one finished item per world per turn
items: A world now finishes one item from its build queue a turn. Rushing the first item no longer lets the world's stockpiled industry finish everything behind it at once. Industry left over goes into the next item, which finishes the turn after, so nothing is wasted.

changes.title: Dominion: portraits found by name
items: The table server now lists the pictures in the music bucket's peoples/ folder, and the game and the Peoples page use them by their real names. Any of png, jpg, jpeg, webp, gif or avif works, in any capitalisation, named after the empire or its people (mirrun.png, Human.jpeg, Ozhvek.webp).
Each picture's address carries a version tag, so a picture replaced or uploaded after the page first looked for it shows at once instead of waiting out the cache.

changes.title: Dominion: clearer travel times
items: A fleet's route on the map now shows a numbered marker where it will stop at the end of each turn, so it's plain when corridor jumps carry it a long way in one turn. A jump along a corridor costs one move however long it is (a quarter of a move with Corridor theory).

Travel times are counted step by step, the way fleets actually move, so a route through nebulae no longer shows a turn too few. The route label, the fleet panel and the order's message all use the same count.

changes.title: Dominion: bug reports, crash recovery, and steadier music
items: Menu → Download a bug report saves a file with any errors the game recorded, your browser, the game's settings, its recent log and your save, plus a note of what happened, so a problem can be played back and fixed. The game keeps a log of the last 40 errors in your browser.
If a turn fails partway, the game goes back to exactly where it was before End turn, explains what happened, and offers the bug report, instead of sticking on Thinking.

Music: a song that won't load now plays from the table server's copy at normal volume (before, it could play silently, or stop the music altogether). A song that stalls is skipped. If several fail in a row, the music stops and says so, and Next track tries again. Music problems are recorded in the bug report.

changes.title: Dominion: fix for End turn sticking on Thinking
items: Fixed End turn freezing on Thinking… partway through a game. The tribute a computer player demands from another empire shared its name with the pirates' tribute demand, and in the built game the pirates' version replaced it, so the turn crashed. Saved games are unaffected: reload the page and carry on.
The build now stops if two parts of the game use the same name, so this kind of clash can't slip through again.

changes.title: Dominion: painted portraits from the music bucket
items: Painted portraits now come from the music bucket's peoples/ folder instead of the game's files. Upload a square image named after an empire (for example peoples/mirrun.png, or .webp or .jpg) and it shows at once on the Peoples page, in the people picker and on the Diplomacy tab, with no rebuild. Empires without one keep their drawing.

changes.title: Dominion: three new empires, and the peoples' portraits
items: Three new empires from the Fracture Lines setting. The Mirrun Commonwealth (Pelagic scholars): +20% science, Ocean worlds hold 3 more population, and they start on an ocean world. The Ylith Aeries (Far sight): ships and worlds see 2 hexes farther, and scouts and colony ships move 1 faster. The Zhaq Free Republics (Never again): garrisons half again as strong that never weaken under siege, and besieged worlds starve half as fast.
Each new empire has its own leader and voice, ship classes and outlines, admirals, directives and computer-player character. Up to 4 rivals are drawn from all eight.

Every people now has a portrait on a hex token, drawn from the setting's descriptions. They appear in the people picker, on the Diplomacy tab, on the token sheet (hex tokens to mark whose a world is), and on a new Peoples page with each people's looks, trait, leader and ships.
Painted art can replace the drawings: the Peoples page has an image-generator prompt for each people, and a square picture named after the empire in the game's art folder is used on the Peoples page.

changes.title: Dominion: computer players use influence
items: Computer players now use influence on each other and on you, at most once every 12 turns each, in keeping with their character. A weak power facing a much stronger neighbour sends gifts or makes amends. One losing a war pays a friend to join it. One that resents the leader or the Corridor Engine's holder denounces them to others. Strong powers squeeze tribute from weak ones.
You're told when a rival sends you a gift, makes amends to you, or denounces you.
Two new computer-player options on the new-game form: Use influence (on at every difficulty) and Demand tribute from you (off on Easy).

changes.title: Dominion: influence in diplomacy, and a space travel guide
items: Influence, on each power's card on the Diplomacy tab. Gifts of credits or exotics raise their regard, though gifts close together count for less. You can make amends for a grievance they remember. Each proposal shows whether they'd accept, and you can sweeten it with credits.

Pressure: demand tribute from a power whose fleet is far weaker than yours (they pay or refuse, and resent it either way), denounce a rival to a third power, or ask a power to join your war, free if they like you, for credits if they're only lukewarm.

How to play has a new Space travel section: ship speeds, open space, corridors, nebulae, rifts, sealed sectors, collapses, the Gate Shard and Engine gate, fuel and supply, and engagements. The strategy guide covers influence in general terms.

changes.title: Dominion: withdrawing, detaching ships, decisive orbital guns, updated guides
items: Engaged fleets: a fleet sharing a hex with enemy warships, or with an enemy world's guns, can't simply sail away. Withdraw pulls it out: it fights the next battle's first exchange defensively, then falls back toward its nearest world. Computer players withdraw from battles they're clearly losing.
Detach and send: choose exactly how many ships of each type to take from a fleet, then send them to a world or at an enemy. In a battle you can detach some ships and withdraw just those.

Orbital guns no longer stalemate: they fire first in each exchange and finish off the most damaged ship. Knocking out a world's guns now counts toward winning the battle, and the battle report says so.
The strategy guide has new sections on fuel and supply, battles and withdrawing, sealed sectors and collapses, and settings and music. The in-game How to play and the tutorial cover the same.
Music on the website, the fan sites and in Dominion now plays from the music bucket's public, cached address, falling back to the table server if needed.

changes.title: Dominion: corridor collapses are rarer, and hit harder
items: A corridor now fails from turn 70, every 60 to 90 turns: about twice in a standard game. Everyone gets 5 turns' warning.
It's always one of the corridors that matter most: the one with the longest way round without it, between settled worlds (most of all, between two powers).
Charting a new route takes a scout resting 3 turns near either end, and it's worth 60 research.

changes.title: Dominion: fuel reserve, sealed sectors, corridor collapses
items: A fuel reserve for every power, shown in the top bar. Colonies make a little fuel, a capital and gas giants more, and fuel depots and stations make the most. Each depot also lets you store 15 more. Fleets moving in supply, refuelling, filling tankers and burning hard all use it, and a short reserve slows your fleets. Raiding a depot steals from its owner's reserve.
Burn hard: a moving fleet can go a hex a turn faster, paid for from the reserve in supply or from its own tank beyond supply. Computer players burn hard to relieve a world under siege.

Sealed sectors: the Dead Zone and the Warden Graveyard can't be entered until a power researches Rift drives (a new Physics technology), or someone lights a Rift beacon on a world within 3 hexes of the sector (200 credits, 10 exotics). A beacon opens the sector to everyone and adds a corridor into it.

Corridor collapses: from turn 45, every 25 to 40 turns, a corridor fails, with 4 turns' warning and a red line on the map. It's never a world's last corridor. A scout that rests near either end charts a new corridor and earns 40 research. Collapses can be turned off on the new-game form.
Long games run faster.

changes.title: Dominion: new sectors
items: The map grows in a long game. From turn 110, three rings of new space open beyond the rim. An open game opens another sector every 80 turns, up to four in all; a standard game gets one.

Each sector has its own character. The Corsair Reach is held by pirate havens and rich in exotics. The Warden Graveyard is full of ruins guarded by Warden husks, whose wrecks pay in research. The Golden Frontier has rich, open, good worlds and no guards. The Dead Zone has no corridors, thick nebula, and few worlds, almost all of them with exotics.
Every power hears 10 turns ahead which sector is coming. The Objectives tab tracks the sector that's coming and the ones already open, and a system's panel says which sector it's in.
New sectors can be turned off on the new-game form. The pirate and creature sectors only come when the game has pirates and creatures.
Long games run faster: the supply check now looks only at nearby worlds.

changes.title: Dominion: extended play for music
items: Give a track extended play in the dominion folder's tracks.json: "repeat": 3 plays it three times in a row, and "loop": true keeps it looping until the game's mood changes. Repeats are seamless.
The Menu's music card has a Loop this track switch for whatever is playing, and shows "play 2 of 3" or "looping".
The main theme can repeat, but never loops forever, so the game's mood always takes over.

changes.title: Dominion: a main theme
items: Dominion can play a main theme when it starts up: on the title screen, or in a new game's first turn. Name the track "theme - ….mp3" in the dominion music folder.
The theme plays once per visit, through to its end, and then the game's own mood takes over: exploration, war or crisis.

changes.title: Dominion: send all your ships somewhere in one click
items: Every explored system's panel now has a "Send your ships here" section. "Send all warships" sends every fleet with a warship in it, including the transports and tankers travelling with them. "Send every ship" sends everything you have.
Each fleet sets out by the quickest way, at its own speed. The message says how long the last one will take, and whether any can't find a way.
"Undo the last send" puts every fleet back to what it was doing, until you end the turn.
It works for your own worlds, empty systems, and an enemy's world you want to attack.

changes.title: Dominion: the Wardens, a persistent threat
items: The Signs: about 35 turns before the Wardens wake, dormant Warden Watchers surface by the rifts one by one, armed and watching, while transmissions on every band grow more urgent. Destroy them while they sleep, for research and one less Node later.

The Wardens spread like an empire. The Heart wakes with Nodes of its own around it, every Watcher still standing wakes as a Node, and every world they burn to rock becomes a new Node. Each Node sends out hunters.
They threaten everyone: one wave in three goes for the strongest power, and half of them go for anyone building the Corridor Engine, the corridors they were made to guard.

Harder to kill: the Heart can't be harmed while its own Nodes stand. Nodes and the Heart can only be worn down over several battles, and they mend only when no one is besieging them. Their strength follows the whole galaxy's combined fleets.
They come back: break the Heart while a Node still stands, and a new Heart, a quarter stronger, grows there after 30 turns. It's over only when the Heart and every Node are gone.

New Objectives-tab states for the Signs and for a broken Heart with Nodes still standing, a NODE marker on the map, research for destroying Watchers and Nodes, and the new machines on the token sheet.
In test games the Wardens now hold out for about 20–45 turns after waking (around 30 on average), where before they were broken in about 13.

changes.title: Dominion: music
items: Dominion plays music now. Tracks come from the dominion folder of the music bucket, and the mood follows the game: exploration in peacetime, war while you're at war, crisis once the Wardens wake.
Name tracks by mood: "exploration - 01.mp3", "war - 01.mp3", "crisis - 01.mp3". Anything else plays in any mood.
Tracks are shuffled, so the same one doesn't come round twice in a row, and a change of mood fades into the next track.
The ♪ button in the top bar turns the music on or off. The Menu has the volume, a Next track button, and what's playing. Your settings are remembered.

changes.title: Dominion: provocation brings war, early game or not
items: A computer power that's truly provoked no longer waits for the early-war turn. That means its regard for you has fallen to −40 or worse, or you've committed a grave offence against it, such as breaking an alliance, in the last 20 turns.
It still needs to feel strong enough to attack. Ordinary friction, like crowded borders or a refused trade, still waits until turn 50 on Normal (60 on Easy, 35 on Hard).

changes.title: Dominion: a calmer early game
items: The computer players no longer race to out-arm each other early on. Until about turn 75, a computer power that's at war with no one keeps a defensive fleet and builds up its worlds instead, then eases into the usual arms race.
They start no wars of their own before turn 50 on Normal (60 on Easy, 35 on Hard). If you attack them, they arm as usual.
In test games, computer rivals' fleets at turn 60 were about a quarter smaller than before, with more buildings. By turn 80 they're back to full strength.
To keep their stronger economies from ending the game sooner, they don't start building the Corridor Engine before turn 100 on Normal (120 on Easy, 80 on Hard). Games last about as long as before.
The Vael were never building faster than anyone else. Their ships move farther and heal anywhere, which makes their fleets seem to be everywhere.

changes.title: Dominion: earlier victories are remembered
items: If you win and keep ruling, the Objectives tab now shows the victory you played on from, for example "Won by the Corridor Engine on turn 133".
The end-of-game screen shows it too, when you finally retire or the game ends.

changes.title: Dominion: the strategy guide, made general
items: The strategy guide no longer gives specific advice: no build orders, research lists, fleet sizes or numbers to follow.

It covers the principles and the important steps to stay competitive instead: how the game is won, the early, middle and late game, choosing a path to victory, playing to your people's strengths, war, defense, threats, exploration, diplomacy, and common mistakes.
For how each rule works, it points to How to play in the game's Menu.

changes.title: Dominion: a strategy guide
items: A new strategy guide (Menu → Strategy guide, or /dominion/strategy.html): how you win and lose, and an opening for your first 30 turns that works for every people.

Three complete plans to follow: the Corridor Engine (every technology in order, with its cost), conquest (fleets, sieges, troops, supply and refits), and the highest score. Plus a plan for holding the Engine in open games.
Each people's best plan, and how the economy, battles (with hit chances), defense, pirates, creatures and the Wardens, exploring, diplomacy and difficulty work.
A list of common mistakes.
Its numbers come from the game's own data, so they stay right when the rules change.

changes.title: Dominion: each people's own ships, and a new token sheet
items: Every people now builds its ships in its own style, with its own outlines and class names. The Concord fly Aegis-class cruisers and Sovereign-class dreadnoughts; the Tessan, Magistrates and Dynasts; the Kel, Mandibles and Hivemothers; the Hegemony, Praetors and Imperators; the Vael, Mantas and Abyssals. All eight ship types have names.
What each ship does is the same for everyone. Only the look and the name change.
The map, the fleet panels, the build list and the battle reports all use them.
The fuel tanker and the traders' merchant convoys have their own outlines now.

A new printable token sheet: a page for each people's ships, a table of every class name, tokens for the traders, pirates, creatures and Wardens, and markers for orbital stations, batteries and fuel depots.

changes.title: Dominion: difficulty choices for the computer players
items: Easy, Normal and Hard are now presets for what the computer players do. Each option can be changed on the new-game form, under Computer players, and the difficulty then shows as Custom.
Strength, meaning fleet size and how readily they go to war: Gentle 0.7×, Standard 1× or Fierce 1.35×.
Build deep-space stations (Hard): computer players put stations in open space on the approaches toward a rival, about one per four colonies and four at most.
Fortify frontier outposts (Normal and Hard), Raid your fuel depots (Normal and Hard), and Form coalitions against the Engine holder (all three).
Pay pirates instead of fighting (Easy and Normal). On Hard they always fight.
The choices are fixed for the game. Games saved earlier use their difficulty's preset.

changes.title: Dominion: deep-space stations
items: With Orbital shipyards, an outpost ship in an empty hex of open space can build a deep-space station there. It uses up the ship and costs 135 credits. It can't be built in a rift or with hostile ships present.

A deep-space station works like an outpost with an Orbital station: light guns, repairs, sight, supply for your fleets, fuel sales, and territory. It's shown on the map as a square, named after the nearest system.
It can be invaded, blockaded and bombarded like any outpost. If its station is destroyed, the site is gone.

changes.title: Dominion: shipyards do early refits
items: Any Shipyard now refits ships with the early systems (Deep sensors, Fold drives and Deflector shields) when they end a turn there.
Everything later (Targeting computers, the ship prototypes, Composite armor, Fire control, Drive tuning) still needs a Drydock.
The refit buttons and the standing order send ships to the nearest place that can fit what they're missing: a shipyard if it's only early systems, otherwise a drydock.

changes.title: Dominion: sending ships for refits
items: The Empire tab has a Refits card that counts your out-of-date ships, and a ⚙ refit tag on each fleet that has them.
"Send all out-of-date ships to drydock" splits them off their fleets and sends them to the nearest drydock that can refit, in one click.
A fleet's panel can send the whole fleet to the drydock, or just its out-of-date ships.
A standing order (on or off, in the Refits card): idle fleets with out-of-date ships go to the nearest drydock by themselves. Fleets told to hold position stay put.

changes.title: Dominion: research reaches ships at a drydock
items: Ships now carry the systems their power had researched when they were built: sensors, drives, shields, targeting, armor, fire control, fuel tanks and the ship prototypes.

New ships are built with everything you've researched. Ships already in service get new research only by ending a turn at one of your Drydocks, where they're refitted at no cost and new armor is added to their hull. It can't happen while enemy warships hold the drydock's orbit.
A fleet's panel says which ships need a refit and how far the nearest drydock is.
The drydock's class upgrades (frigate to cruiser, cruiser to dreadnought) are gone.
Your existing ships keep everything you'd researched before this update.
The computer powers research Orbital shipyards early, build a drydock at their capital, and send out-of-date fleets there before going on the attack.

changes.title: Dominion: stations and drydocks do different jobs
items: Orbital stations are forward bases: ships there now repair 2 hull a turn, not to full. Their guns, sight and supply are unchanged.

The Drydock is the home yard. Ships there still repair to full every turn, ships built at that world now cost 15% less, and ships there can be refitted a class up: a frigate into a cruiser, or a cruiser into a dreadnought.
A refit costs the difference in price, paid in credits and exotics, and the ship comes out at full hull. Refits are on the fleet panel.
Every world of yours still repairs your ships 1 hull a turn.
The computer powers refit ships at their drydocks when they're rich.

changes.title: Dominion: outposts sell fuel and exotics
items: An outpost with a fuel depot or station sells fuel: +2 credits a turn, or +3 on a gas giant.
An outpost on an exotics deposit exports them: +2 credits a turn, on top of the exotics it produces.
Merchant convoys refuel at outposts with a depot or station within a hex of their route, paying the owner 2 credits each time.
A blockaded outpost sells nothing, and neither does one whose depot has been raided dry.
Each outpost's panel shows what it earns.

changes.title: Dominion: orbital stations, and guns over outposts
items: Orbital station (needs Orbital shipyards, 90): build one over a colony or an outpost. It has light guns (4 hull, one shot of 2, or +4 hull added to a battery's).
Ships at a station are repaired to full each turn. The station sees 2 hexes farther, and gives supply like a fuel depot.
Outposts can now have an Orbital battery or an Orbital station. Outposts have no industry, so you buy these with credits from the outpost's panel: 150 for a battery, 135 for a station.
The computer powers fortify outposts near their enemies when they're at war.

changes.title: Dominion: pirate ransom and tribute, patrol pacts, depot raids, and the Free Traders
items: Pirates demand payment: a ransom when their raiders hold one of your worlds, and tribute when a haven sets up near you. Pay and that haven's raiders leave all your worlds alone for 20 turns; refuse and they come anyway.

Pirate patrol pacts (Diplomacy tab): partners' warships guard each other's worlds from raiders, and each gets half the bounty when the other destroys a pirate ship. The computer powers propose and form them.
Depot raids: at war, warships holding an enemy fuel depot's system can raid it. They fill their own tanks and tankers, and the depot gives its owner no supply for 5 turns.
The Free Traders: merchant convoys run between colonies with an Exchange, paying both worlds' owners when they arrive. Pirates hunt convoys with no warships beside them.
Traders who reach your worlds sometimes offer a deal: exotics, a used frigate, star charts, or a rumor of where a relic lies.
Relics are no longer hidden right next to a homeworld.

changes.title: Dominion: choose how many pirates and creatures
items: A new setting, Pirates and creatures, with three levels: None, Light or Heavy. Choose it when you start a game, or change it at any time from the Menu.
Light is the default: one pirate haven at a time (two on large maps) with one raider fleet, a couple of crystal swarms, and one void leviathan from turn 70. Heavy keeps the full numbers.
Turning it down mid-game removes the extra havens, raiders and swarms at once, those nearest the settled worlds first. None removes them all.
Games saved earlier switch to Light.
Raiders who lose a ship at a world stay away from it for 15 turns, so defending a world drives them off.

changes.title: Dominion: pirates no longer stop expansion
items: Pirate havens first appear on turn 30 (was 14).
Raiders only go after established colonies (population 3 or more, founded at least 12 turns ago). Outposts and new colonies are left alone.
Pirates and crystal swarms never fire on unarmed ships, so colony ships, outpost ships, scouts, transports and tankers pass safely. A swarm still keeps anyone from settling its own system.
A pirate or creature blockade no longer starves a world or starts the surrender clock: it halves yields and stops growth only while it lasts.
Pirates and creatures had cut how far the powers spread by about a third by turn 60. Now it's about 3%.

changes.title: Dominion: relics of the old empires, and the Outer Reach
items: Eleven relics, one of each, hidden in ruins and anomalies. The first fleet to end its turn at one recovers it, and it's kept at the finder's capital. Each is worth 10 score.
A relic belongs to the world that keeps it: take the world and you take its relics. If the world is destroyed, they lie there, or nearby, for anyone to find.

The Founders' Star Chart expands the galaxy. Read it once and four rings of uncharted space, the Outer Reach, open beyond the rim, with new systems linked into the corridors and four more relics to find.
The Gate Shard opens a new corridor from one of your worlds every 15 turns.
The rest work by being held: faster ships, repairs anywhere, the whole map charted, more industry, science or credits, stronger guns, more population room, and protection against the Wardens.
The computer powers read the Star Chart as soon as they find it, and use the Gate Shard to link their capital to their farthest worlds.

changes.title: Dominion: the Corridor Engine in open games
items: In an open game, finishing the Corridor Engine no longer ends the game. Its holder gets free corridor travel, a gate that jumps one fleet from the Engine world to any of its worlds every 5 turns, +2 credits on every colony, and 2 score a turn.
Only one Engine can stand. Others already under construction wait, with their work kept.
Capture the Engine world and the Engine is yours. Hold its orbit with its guns down and a barrage destroys it, and the race to build one starts again.
While enemy warships hold the Engine's orbit, it gives its holder nothing.
The computer powers resent the holder, and once it has held the Engine a while they form a coalition against it.
Standard 200-turn games are unchanged: finishing the Engine wins.

changes.title: Dominion: advances, anomalies, new buildings, pirates and monsters
items: Advances: once a technology is done, research builds on it a level at a time: +5% industry, science or credits a level (to 5), +1 warship hull or skill (to 2), +1 population room (to 3), +2 fuel (to 3). Each level costs more. Science never runs out of use.
More ways to research: anomalies (✦ on the map) that a scout surveys for 40–160 research, research pacts (+5% science per trade treaty, up to three), and the wrecks of pirates and creatures.
Four new buildings: Garrison barracks, Deep-space observatory (studies nearby anomalies without a ship), Drydock (full repairs every turn) and Orbital habitat (+2 population room).
Pirate havens appear near the settled worlds from turn 14 and send out raiders that blockade weak worlds and steal credits. Burn a haven for 100 credits and 50 research.
Crystal swarms guard rich and exotic systems from the start: clear one to settle there. Void leviathans drift in from turn 40 and feed on unguarded worlds. Both pay research when destroyed.

changes.title: Dominion: Orbital batteries that defend a world
items: The Orbital battery is a fortress now: 6 hull (8 with the shield grid), two shots a round at skill 13 for 2 damage each, and it repairs 2 hull a turn when no enemy holds the orbit. It costs 100 (was 70). Before, two cruisers silenced it every time without losing a ship; now two frigates or a lone cruiser die against it, and it takes a real fleet to bring it down.

While a world's guns stand, a siege can't blockade it: full industry, credits, trade and growth, and the siege clock (hunger, surrender) only starts once the guns are silent. Enemy warships in orbit still stop repairs, so a fleet that holds on wears the guns down.
A battery's troops add 2 to the world's garrison against invasion.
The world panel shows the guns' hull against their full strength, and the siege panel says whether the blockade has started.

changes.title: Dominion: fuel tankers, and supply lines to defend
items: Fuel tankers (any shipyard, 50): they carry 12 units of fuel. Travelling with a fleet, one tops up the tank when it runs dry, so the fleet reaches farther. Parked, it's a supply point: your fleets within 2 hexes stay in supply, a unit of its fuel each a turn. It fills up again in supply at home.
Supply lines can be cut: enemy warships in a supply point's system (a parked tanker, a fuel depot, a besieged colony) stop it giving supply. Tankers are unarmed, so escort them.
Tankers have their own muster point, and the computer powers bring one behind their main war fleet.

changes.title: Dominion: fuel and fuel depots
items: Fleets carry fuel: their thirstiest ship's tank, in turns of travel beyond supply (scouts 10, frigates and colony ships 6, cruisers and transports 5, dreadnoughts 4). Each turn a fleet moves beyond supply burns one; out of fuel it crawls a hex a turn. In supply it refuels. The Vael's living hulls need none.
Fuel depots: an outpost now gives supply only with one. Claim an outpost with its depot (40 credits), or build one there later (60 credits). A colony always gives supply.
A fleet's panel shows its fuel, and warns when a course ends beyond supply with too little in the tank.
The computer powers build depots and keep their attacks within reach of their fuel.

changes.title: Dominion: muster points for new ships
items: Standing orders for where new ships go: all of them, or warships, troop transports, colony and outpost ships or scouts on their own, to a world or outpost of yours. A kind's own order overrides the one for all ships.
Set them in the Empire tab's Strategic orders, or from a world's own panel (Send warships here). New ships leave as soon as they're built and join their kind waiting there.
A muster point that's taken or razed is struck off, and you're told.

changes.title: Dominion: managing big fleets
items: A fleet's ships are listed by type, with how many and their hull together; each ship's hull is a click away.
Split off by type: one, half or all of a type into a new fleet, the most damaged first (to send the wounded home); the admiral stays.
Join all here: every fleet of yours in a system joins the selected one in a click.
The Empire tab lists war fleets apart from scouts, transports and colony ships, with where each is, and folds a long list away.

changes.title: Dominion: trade, an exotics market, and real sieges
items: Trade: each colony earns credits from trade links, other colonies within 4 hexes that are yours or a treaty partner's; an Exchange doubles it.
An exotics market (with an Exchange): buy at the price, sell for three quarters of it; every unit moves the price, which drifts back.

Sieges have a cost: a besieged world makes half its industry and credits, trades and grows nothing, loses a population every 3 turns, and its garrison weakens toward half, so landings get easier. After 10 turns an ordinary colony starved to 3 population surrenders; a capital never does.
The computer powers send fleets to break sieges of their worlds, and use the market. In all-computer games worlds now change hands (5 to 8 in a typical war), by landings and surrenders.

changes.title: A Difficulty setting for the GM
items: The GM view's Map and fight tab has a Difficulty card: Standard, Tough (+1 to the threats' attack targets and one more box), Hard (+2 and two boxes, and one more foe in each group) and Deadly (+3 and three boxes, two more in each group). A minor foe keeps its one box.

It applies to threats as they're added: in the Encounter panel, on the battle map, and when a playtest sets up a scene. It's the core's rule for a tougher version, for every threat at once, in every setting and both fan games.

changes.title: Aurora's playtest: good guys against bad guys
items: Dead Air is rewritten as a clear heroes-against-villains case, to teach the game: save a terrified girl and forty commuters on a stalled train, find out who's behind the blackout, and stop him.

A new villain, Overcharge (Class IV), the Foundation's enforcer, sets the trap for Subject 19. The investigation pays off in the fight: take out the girl's tag and his force field drops from IV to III.
Sergei Grachyov no longer offers a trade; he watches from the platform at the end, a hook for later. The case ends with the girl home and the villain in cuffs.
The run sheet, the Campaign tab's outline, people and places, and the battle map's tokens (with a prompt for Overcharge's) follow the new story.

changes.title: Dominion: sieges work, and a targeted barrage
items: A world's orbital guns used to repair a point at the end of every turn, straight after the battle that knocked them out, so its orbit was never clear and troops could never land on a world with a battery or a capital.

Now a world under siege (an enemy's warships in its orbit) can't repair its guns, launch the ships it finishes, or raise a new battery: keep your warships in orbit through the end of a turn, and your transports can land the next.

Targeted barrage: a fleet holding an enemy world's orbit can destroy one of its buildings a turn. The Shipyard takes the ships in its yards with it; no population is lost. The computer powers use it too.
The invasion panel says how.

changes.title: USS Pelion and Grimm on the shared rules
items: Both fan games are rebuilt on the shared character creator and the current core rules, like the four settings: what changes in the core now reaches them too.
Species and heritages follow the core: bonuses only, nobody starts below 10; ready-made characters are refit to match (each keeps their best attribute). USS Pelion's crew now spend 3 Edges.

Pelion keeps its phaser power and settings, the ship's systems, Power, Torpedoes and the concussive damage roll, its ranks, the Starfleet Command track and library records; Grimm keeps the woge, its Wesen and Lenses, spells, rituals and charms, and its Trouble tracks, and gains lore cards.
What a player saved in the old pages carries over, and old character files still load.

changes.title: Aurora: super-speed by range band, and one Fallout track
items: Speed, Flight and Super Leaping move by range band, never yards on the battle map: the sheet, the GM's cards and the table show the band (Class I to Medium, II to Long, III to Extreme, IV and up anywhere in the scene) beside the move on foot.
A new Super-speed fight range track on the battle map: the first lane is the fight itself, and each lane out is a range band from it.

Collateral, Scrutiny and Backlash are now one shared Fallout track of 6 boxes. Each mark is one of the three kinds; how many boxes are marked sets how bad it is, and the kind with the most marks says what form it takes. Clearing removes a mark of its own kind.
Tracks saved under the old names join Fallout as marks of their kind.

changes.title: Consistency pass: core rules and the four settings
items: Core: success margin doesn't increase damage unless a weapon's own entry says so (as the core's homebrew rules and the Shattered Crown's greatweapons already allowed).
Aurora: its own scale for Operant threats (attacks 14-17, Dodge 9-14, 3-6 boxes, 7-8 for the most powerful), beside the core's guidelines for ordinary foes.
Aurora: the quick reference gives Class V and VI damage and Toughness boxes.
The creator no longer shows the creation checklist for the GM's characters (notable Operants and extras), which are built from stat blocks.

changes.title: Aurora: Toughness boxes, and harm above Class IV
items: A hero gets one Toughness box for each Class of their best Defense (Toughness, a Force Field, an Aegis suit). Toughness boxes are marked before the three Injury boxes, carry no penalty, and clear when the fight ends.
Against anyone with more than 3 boxes, Class V attacks mark 4 boxes and Class VI mark 5, before Defense.
An Aegis suit now gives its Toughness II (physical and energy) in the GM view's encounters, as the guide says.
The sheet, the GM cards, the battle map tokens and the shared table show the Toughness boxes; ending an encounter clears them.

changes.title: Aurora: a telling hit gets through any Defense
items: An attack at or below a Defense's Class still marks 1 box on a telling hit (made by 5 or more, or a natural 3 or 4). Attacks a Class above it still mark a box fewer, and a telling one always marks at least 1.
This is Aurora's one exception to the core rule that a telling hit never adds boxes.
In test fights the party went from never beating a Defense IV-VI villain to winning 93% against Steel Hawk, about 80% against Helios and Grachyov, and 43-44% against Autuarch and the Atomic Man.

changes.title: Alternate forms with their own numbers
items: Any character can have their own alternate form (Powers step): its name and their normal shape's, attribute, Dodge and Move changes, the powers that work only in the form, and a note.

The sheet's and the table card's form switch, skills, Dodge, Move and the Encounter panel all use the form's numbers while the character is in it; a form-only power gives no attack, Defense or move outside it.

changes.title: Aurora: every notable Operant as a ready-made sheet
items: Eight supers the history names now have stat blocks: Herbert Unler, Zarloff the Elder, the Ivory Phoenix, Charlie Swift, Warlord I, Armageddon, Johnny Vanroy (Mr. Power) and John Marcus Mars Jr.
All 30 named Operants are ready-made sheets for the GM, built from their stat blocks; the GM view adds them as NPCs. Mr. Marvel, Uathach and the Ice Reaper come with their alternate forms.

changes.title: Aurora: Piercing, and the neurogun
items: Piercing (armor-piercing rounds): a piercing attack meets a Defense one Class higher than it is, but marks its own Class's boxes. Armor with a Defense rating protects as usual; a plain body armor vest doesn't help against it.

The flechette rifle is Class II, Piercing. The neurogun is an advanced taser: a Class II physical stun, Body −4 to stay up, which Defense II stops. A stun weapon with a Class now meets Defense like any other attack.

changes.title: Aurora: damage types and the Vulnerability complication
items: Four damage types: physical, energy, mystic and mind. Each Defense covers its own (Toughness physical; Force Field physical and energy); against another type it counts one Class lower. No Defense but Mind Defense helps against the mind, and force made by the mind is physical.
Weak (a box more), resistant (Defense +1) and immune (nothing below Class VI) to a type, element or material. The Vulnerability complication is a weakness chosen with the GM.

changes.title: Aurora: Defense takes an attack one Class above it
items: An attack must be at least one Class above a Defense to do anything, and then marks one box fewer; an equal or lower one does nothing (before, an equal attack marked a box fewer and a higher one hit in full). Falls follow: Toughness II walks away from a rooftop, IV from a tower, V from a fall from a plane.

changes.title: Aurora: unstable powers come in levels
items: Unstable I flares on a natural 18 with Powers, II on 17–18, III on 16–18, IV on 15–18. Lab-made gives Unstable II; the Unstable Powers complication gives the level chosen (I to III); the two add, to IV. The GM can raise or lower a level in play, and Strain 3 flares any power on 16–18.

changes.title: Aurora: the Foundation's retrieval teams, and Dead Air
items: Retrieval teams carry neuroguns, flechette rifles and stun grenades besides their tranquilizers and dampening net, and will kill to leave no witnesses (a Foundation hardware table in the GM's Guide).
The first case is now Dead Air, and Subject 19 has no codename.

changes.title: No one starts below 10
items: Origins only raise attributes, and their bonuses come out of the five attribute points, so every origin starts with the same total. Custom and homebrew origins: 0 to +2 each, +3 at most.
Ordinary people: 10 in every attribute, Dodge 8, Move 5 yards, 6 in anything untrained. An attribute drops below 10 only for a reason in play: an injury, a curse, a form.
The pregenerated characters are rebalanced to match, and older characters are put right when they're opened.

changes.title: The GM view: NPCs, powers on the cards, and the playtests in one click
items: NPCs (the people the characters meet) are full characters in the GM view, from any threat or written in: their own boxes, portrait and token, linked to their battle map token, and on their own side in the Encounter panel.
Table cards list powers by Class and spells, show a power's move apart from the move on foot, and label the injury boxes; the same character isn't added twice unless they're a generic NPC.
A playtest loads in one click: its campaign, the ready-made characters, its NPCs, clocks and files, and each scene's map with its enemies (who grow with the adventure's threat).

changes.title: Music, battle maps and character pictures
items: Music for each setting, to play at the table or download; battle maps, tokens and portraits for the playtests, from the table server, with replaced pictures picked up.

changes.title: The settings and the core rules, brought in line
items: What the settings had worked out separately is now in the core rules, for every setting: chases where one side is clearly faster, chases by range (an opposed roll moves the range a band), and a damage track for vehicles; acting first and acting more than once a round; helping in a fight; pins that hold against someone much stronger.
Falls mark boxes by height (a story 1, a rooftop 2, a tower 3 and Dying, higher is certain death), with fire and foul air beside them. Every setting's fall uses it; Aurora's adds Classes.

Conditions, defined once: stunned, Frightened (keep away from the source, −2 against it, Will each turn to shake it) and Charmed. The settings' fear spells and horrors (Grave Chill, Dread, the Thing from the Deep, Emotion Control) now say Frightened.

Weapons: what "3, and Dying" means, explosions, stun weapons and jams; and armor, toughness, weaknesses and materials, the way every setting's gear and threats already use them. Guns now jam on a natural 18 in Trails of Blood & Dust too, as in the other settings.

Investigation: a head start (a character trained in the right field skips Confront) and a rival clock, from Fracture Lines; and enemies' files on the characters (+2 when it applies, destroyed when found), from Aurora, now in every setting's GM view.

Tracks: shared and personal tracks described once. A Mind track (Aurora's mental harm) is described as an option any setting can use; its middle box is now Overwhelmed, since Reeling is the Shattered Crown's word for stunned.
Smaller fixes: The Shattered Crown's Charm is resisted with Will (it said Presence), as everywhere else; Fracture Lines' ship fights are described as they're actually run.

changes.title: Aurora: mind powers, a Mind track and Mind Defense
items: Every character has a Mind track of three boxes beside the injury track: Shaken (−1 to mental actions), Overwhelmed (−2), Broken (unconscious or catatonic). Psychic attacks mark it; it never leaves anyone Dying, and a night's sleep clears it. It's on the play tab, the printed sheet, the GM view's cards and the battle map.

Mind Defense from Telepathy, Mind Control, Possession or an ExLAW psi-dampening headset: a weaker mind power does nothing, an equal one is resisted at +2. A Class IV mind against someone without it is resisted at −2.
Psychic attacks: Telepathy II (a psychic stab) and Illusion III (fears made real), one Class below the power, Powers against Will, never Dodge, Toughness or Force Field.

Rules for reading minds (and being noticed), mind links, being controlled (the player keeps playing; +2 against a harmful command, +4 against hurting a friend; Spark for another roll), emotions, illusions and sensing lies.

The Encounter panel resolves psychic attacks as Will contests on the Mind track (Lord Marrow's nightmare no longer meets Toughness or Dodge), and the sheet's roller applies the Mind penalty to mental actions.

changes.title: Aurora: speed, flight, height and falling
items: Speed, Flight and Super Leaping move a range band in a fight: Medium at Class I, Long at II, Extreme at III, anywhere in the scene from IV. The sheet's Move shows it.

Speed's steps, evened out: acts first (I), a second defense and blows at speed (II), two actions once a scene (III), two actions a round (IV), three (V). Blows at speed hit one Class below your Speed. Celerity's now hit at Class III.
Chases against vehicles: a car is Class I, a helicopter II, a jet III, a fighter IV; a higher Class wins without a roll.

Height counts in the distance (and on the battle map, where a token can have a height). Dives hit one Class higher; carrying slows you a Class; a flier stunned, knocked out or knocked back falls unless they make a Powers roll.
A fall is an attack with a Class by its height (I to IV), so Toughness protects against it.
The Encounter panel puts Speed first in the turn order, gives the extra actions and the second defense, offers a Dive to fliers, and warns when a flier falls.

changes.title: Aurora: super strength, and every power's attacks in the Encounter panel
items: Super strength has its own rules: lifting (one step past your Class is a push), objects with a Class to break, throwing (Athletics; a car also hits everyone next to the target), weapons in strong hands (the higher Class; ordinary weapons break above Class II), knockback from Class III, and pins that hold against weaker targets (Body −2 per Class of difference).
Strength and Size give +2 to Body for feats and breaking holds: a new choice in the sheet's roller.

A player character's attack powers now come into the Encounter panel at their Class: Strength (blows and throws), Natural Weapons, Blast, Telekinesis, Elemental and Weather Control, Gravity, Shadow, Manifest and Stretching. Before, a hero with powers fought there with fists and gear only.
The Encounter panel applies strong hands and logs knockback and how hard a pin is to break.

changes.title: Aurora: Exposure, villains' files and team-ups
items: A character with a Secret Identity has Exposure, a track of four boxes: marked when the secret slips, cleared by alibis. When it fills, the hero is unmasked and the player chooses the price. It shows on the play tab and in the GM view.

Exposure is relative: each hero keeps a list of who already knows the secret (family, a team, ExLAW, a villain). A legal status adds its own (Registered: the EMD; Reserve Agent: ExLAW's Director). Exposure measures the secret getting past them, and someone new who learns it goes on the list.
Villains keep files on the heroes: what they know, and +2 against that hero when it applies. The GM records them in the GM view; a hero who finds a file sees it on their sheet, and can destroy it.
Team-ups: two heroes combine powers in one action. The attack counts one Class higher and both mark a box of Strain. The Encounter panel has a Team-up choice for attacks with a Class.

changes.title: Aurora: stats for every named character
items: Every Notable Operant in Aurora's GM's Guide now has a stat block: Class, attacks, Dodge, boxes, Defense, powers, skills and what makes them who they are at the table. Autuarch, master of the White Hand, gets an entry of his own.

All 22 are in the GM view, in the Encounter panel and on the battle map, under their name and Class. Their Defense works as the rules say: an attack below it does nothing, one equal to it marks a box fewer.

changes.title: The campaign builder, with card triggers
items: The GM view has a Campaign tab: the campaign's premise and themes, an outline of adventures, people, places, factions, and sessions (the plan, the log and a recap for the players). Save it to a file, or open one.
Roll any of them from the setting's own tables: adventure seeds, key characters, places, threats, allegiances and names. A rolled entry opens in its form, to change before you keep it.
Triggers: a step of the outline can stay locked until the group holds the cards it names, and as many as you ask for. Then it unlocks for good and tells the GM what happens.

Share any entry with the players: they see its public part on their play tab, through the shared table; never a secret or the GM's notes. A shared locked step shows as locked, and what opens it if the GM says so.

changes.title: The GM view and GM's Guides open to everyone; homebrew origins and advantages
items: Every creator's GM view and GM's Guide are open again, and the GM's Guides are back on the setting pages in Word. A GM access code is needed only to start a shared table on this site: ask for one in the Discord server or by email.

Homebrew now takes origins (tier, attribute changes, origin skills, origin advantages and their complications; in Aurora, powers like one of the setting's origins) and advantages (+2 to a narrow task with a skill). They join the creator's choices like the setting's own.
Want your own table server on Cloudflare? Ask, and we'll send you the package.

changes.title: A dev blog and the community Discord
items: The new Dev blog page carries news from the making of the game: rules changes, the settings, playtest notes and what's coming. Filter it by setting, or read every post.
The home page shows the latest three posts.
Join the Legend Dynamics Discord server from the home page, the Discord page or any page's footer, or at legenddynamicsrpg.com/join.

changes.title: Homebrew: your own threats, weapons, Edges, cards, powers, spells and rituals
items: The GM view has a Homebrew tab: make your own threats, weapons and Edges with simple forms, no code. They work like the setting's own, marked homebrew, in the Encounter panel, on the battle map, in characters' gear and the roller, and in the creator's Edges.

Cards, spells and rituals too: homebrew lore cards, data records, dossiers and tales join the subjects the GM records findings with (and Trails' Hunter's Almanac); homebrew hexes, cantrips and psionic powers, and Aurora's powers (what each does at Class I to VI), join the creator's choices; homebrew rituals make a ritual book beside Rituals by heart.
Players get the GM's homebrew when they join the shared table, or from a homebrew file.

Bonuses the table works out, chosen from menus: a weapon's accuracy, strong hits and what it's made of; a threat's hard hide, weaknesses, what alone can hurt it, how hard it is to hit and a second defense; an Edge's skill, Dodge or Move bonus, a second defense or shrugging off a telling hit; an attack spell, cast in the Encounter panel. The sheet, the roller, the shared table and the Encounter panel use them.
The core rules' Making your own chapter gives the numbers to keep homebrew in line with the book's.

changes.title: Fracture Lines: example data records, the Countdown and skill
items: Seven example data records in the GM's Guide: a Halvane lattice core, the Warden of the Ashkarr, a corridor engine, a spatial fracture, a living hull, corporate black-site encryption and an alien weapon cache, each with what goes wrong in each phase.
The Countdown no longer runs on routine discovery: the GM starts one after a failed roll or a success at a cost, when the stakes are real.
A character trained in the skill that fits the subject can skip Confront the unknown.
Rival clocks: an ordinary danger clock for whoever is racing the crew to the same find.

changes.title: Trails of Blood & Dust: special loads and the hunter's shot
items: Special loads: silver rounds, rock salt shells, cold iron shot, blessed rounds and incendiary shells, tracked as three uses a job each rather than counted bullets. Silver bullets in the gear list become silver rounds.
A load works against the weakness it's made of, whoever fires it. With a lore card for the creature and the matching load, a hunter's shot makes the called shot or effect the card permits.
Coming by loads can cost: buying silver marks Whispers only if folks learn what it's for, and church silver or the makings of fire mark Heat. Blessed rounds burn a demon but never banish it.
A wraith can now be hurt by rock salt in the Encounter panel, as its weakness already said.

changes.title: Legend cards and the price of information
items: A Legend card records one thing the characters have established: the finding, its limits, the evidence or source, how it was learned, what it cost, and who holds it. Each setting names its cards.
A card can be earned by a discovery clock, or directly: seen or tested firsthand, a reliable account, or the subject's own word backed by evidence.
Information is never free: each direct source has a price, ticking the threat clock or a track. A clock's card costs what the clock already cost. Proposing an idea is free.
A real weakness works whether or not anyone holds a card for it.
A new section for the GM: making Legend cards.

changes.title: Fracture Lines, Aurora and The Shattered Crown: data records, dossiers and tales
items: Fracture Lines keeps data records in an archive, Aurora dossiers in a binder, and The Shattered Crown tales in a saga, each with its own chapter in both guides.
The Shattered Crown gains discovery clocks, racing its Doom track.
New advantages give three starting cards the player writes: secrets from their role or origin that aren't common knowledge.
Trails of Blood & Dust: each source of a lore card now has its price.

changes.title: Trails of Blood & Dust: renewing a talisman
items: A broken talisman (the Talisman Edge) is renewed only between jobs, and only by going back to its maker or another worker of the same tradition. Until then it stays spent.

changes.title: Website and editorial improvements
items: A Start here page: choose a setting, create a character, join or run a game.
Shorter Play online section on the home page, linking to the shared-table and Discord pages for setup.
The four settings now call a character's role a role everywhere (the home page and creators said calling). Same choices, same saved characters.
Small wording fixes in the core rules (an origin, a role), and one copyright notice per page.
This changelog, and the rules' last-updated date on the core-rules page.

changes.title: Movement, reach and range bands
items: Tighter range bands: Short 25 yards, Medium 100, Long 300, Extreme 1,000; Close stays 10. Running covers 20 yards.
Move: each character has a Move in yards, worked out from their attributes, Athletics and origin; Run is twice Move.
Weapon reach: every weapon in hand has a reach of 1, 2 or 3 yards.
Injury and hard going slow Move; stepping away from a fight is free.
Telling-hit effects depend on the weapon: Pin needs a weapon in hand, fists or a grapple.
Origin speed adjustments, and mounts and vehicles.

changes.title: Balance revision
items: Fine weapons and tools: +2 to one narrowly defined use of a skill, never a defense.
Additional Defense: a second defense each round at −2.
Magic limits: Quicker hand, every hostile burst names a defense or a resistance, personal magic marks at most 3 boxes, and charms still face the target's defense.
Telling hits: Break gear, Pin, Precise and Knock down clarified, with firm limits.
Medical treatment: one field-treatment and one proper-care attempt per set of injuries.
